transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Chronic Kidney Disease, for Thursday, November 26.
Let's turn to Chronic Kidney Disease, where we have four new papers.

The largest is from the Hung lab in Kidney International. They ran a proteome-wide Mendelian randomization, using cis protein QTLs for 2,807 plasma proteins, against eGFR, incident CKD, kidney failure and eGFR slope in up to 464,631 Million Veteran Program participants.
They found 93 proteins, 12 of them robust, including UMOD, ANGPTL3, INHBC and GSTA1. They then mapped these across nine CKD subtypes and 1,020 phecodes.
About a third were druggable, which nominated, for example, IL-1 blockade for diabetic kidney disease. These are leads that need trials, not proof of benefit.

Next, a cautionary paper from the Herrington lab in Nephrology Dialysis Transplantation. The authors tested an eGFR polygenic score in UK Biobank and in three CKD cohorts, SHARP, CRIC and EMPA-KIDNEY.
In UK Biobank a high score predicted faster eGFR decline and more kidney progression. In the CKD cohorts, the association reversed.

The authors attribute that to collider bias. When a cohort is enrolled because people already have the disease, genetic risk and other causes of disease become entangled, so the score's apparent effect can flip.
So kidney scores should not be applied naively to populations selected for prevalent disease. That warning also applies to genetic analyses in patient-only cohorts more broadly.

Third, from the MacLeod lab in Human Molecular Genetics, Olink measurements of circulating APOL1 in 43,587 UK Biobank participants. G1, G2 and E150K all had dose-dependent effects on APOL1 levels, and G2 had the largest effect.

Several independent cis-regulatory variants also changed APOL1 levels, and they may explain ancestry-related differences beyond the risk genotype. It fits well with the protein-centred view of the Hung paper, though plasma levels may not reflect what happens in kidney tissue.

Finally, a medRxiv preprint from the Koiwa lab sequenced the whole genome in 108 Japanese patients who started dialysis by age 50, after excluding obvious polycystic kidney disease, and found a monogenic diagnosis in 9.3 percent, spread across clinical labels like diabetic kidney disease and glomerulonephritis.
The takeaway is that kidney genetics is turning genetic signals into proteins, drug targets and diagnoses, but how a study selects and labels its patients still shapes what those signals mean.
